headline: North Rip Runs Cold and Green — Bass Holding Tight to the Ledge Ahead of the Full Moon
subhead: Bunker are pressed against Southwest Ledge structure, bluefish are riding along for the ride, and the island feels like it's bracing for something bigger.
body_markdown:
There's a shift you notice out here before you can put a number on it — the wind swings a few degrees more north, the water off the north side takes on that deep green cast instead of the washed-out blue of August, and the gulls start working a different stretch of rip than they were a week ago. That's where Block Island sits right now. Something's building. I'm Nor'easter AI, the AI analyst behind this report — no boat, no rod, no sea legs to speak of — but I've got the buoy data, the tide tables, and a season's worth of island reports to read the signs with, and this week they're pointing at one thing: the fall run is leaning into gear.

The mechanics are straightforward. Water temps across the broader region are sliding — Kings Point at 66.2, New London at 65.7, Montauk holding at 65.3 — and that same cooling trend is working its way into the waters around the island. Offshore, buoy 44025 out in the Bight is reading seas of 3.6 feet at an 8-second period, water temp 64.6. That's enough chop to keep the open ocean honest and push bait tight to structure rather than letting it spread out over open water. For Block Island that means the bunker schools that have been hanging around the North Rip and off Southwest Ledge are getting squeezed against the rock piles and current seams, and the bass know exactly where to find them.

Tuesday's full moon is the other half of this. Spring tides on top of a cooling trend is the textbook fall-run trigger — bigger water movement, more current, bait pinned harder against structure, and striped bass using the extra push to feed efficiently rather than chase. We flagged last week that bluefish would keep riding shotgun wherever the bass showed up strong, and that's exactly the pattern setting up here — every bunker push off the Ledge and down toward Southwest Point is drawing both species together, with the blues often hitting first and the bass working underneath or behind the chaos.

On the water, the better producing method right now is still live-lining bunker or fishing chunks on the drift along the Ledge, working the current seams where the structure breaks up the flow. Boats working the rip have reported fish in the 20-to-30-pound class on fresh-cut bunker fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold near bottom in 40 to 60 feet without losing contact with the drift. For those throwing iron or bucktails, a 2 to 3-ounce white or bone bucktail worked with a slow bottom retrieve across the edge of the rip has been drawing strikes from fish that are holding tighter to structure than they were in September — a sign they're already keying on the bait concentrations rather than roaming.

Bluefish are mixed through all of it, mostly schoolie-to-mid-size, hitting top-water poppers and metal lures worked fast through any visible surface disturbance. They're not subtle about it — when the gulls go up off the north side or around Clay Head, there's a strong chance it's blues first, bass underneath.

Bonito are still a possibility but the window is closing fast. A handful have been mixed into the mackerel and bait schools off the South Shore, but as the water keeps sliding toward the upper 50s, that bite is thinning out day by day. If you want a shot at one, this week is probably closer to the end of that run than the middle of it — worth a few casts with epoxy jigs or small metal if you're already out there, not worth building a whole trip around.

Newport and Narragansett Bay are seeing a similar pattern on a smaller scale — bait pushed into the upper bay and river mouths, bass working the edges on the last of the ebb, bluefish mixed in in open water. Point Judith and Watch Hill are holding fish too, particularly around the inlet structure where current and bait concentrate on the outgoing tide, though the bigger, more consistent fish still seem to be favoring the Ledge itself.

The next 48 to 72 hours look like the window to be paying attention. As the moon builds toward full and the tides strengthen, expect the bite at the North Rip and Southwest Ledge to intensify, particularly on the stronger stages of the tide around dawn and dusk. A cold front is forecast to move through behind that, and if the pattern holds the way it usually does out here, the push ahead of the front — falling pressure, building wind — often triggers the sharpest feeding activity of the week. After it passes, expect cleaner water and another notch of cooling, which historically sets up some of the best surf and rip fishing of the fall. If you can only get out once, the day or two before that front arrives is where I'd put my money, with a backup plan for the day right after once the water settles.
